title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: Left alone, Darya Alexandrovna scanned the room with a good housewife's eye. Everything she had seen on her way through the house, and everything she saw now in her room, gave her an impression of wealth and sumptuousness, of that modern European luxury she had only read about in English novels and never seen in Russia, certainly not in the country. Everything was new — from the new French hangings on the walls to the carpet that covered the whole floor. The bed had a spring mattress, and a special kind of bolster, and silk pillowcases on the little pillows. The marble washstand, the dressing table, the small sofa, the side tables, the bronze clock on the chimney piece, the window curtains, and the _portières_ were all new and expensive.

The smart maid who came in to offer her services — hair piled high, a gown smarter than Dolly's — was as new and expensive as the room itself. Darya Alexandrovna liked her neatness, her deferential and helpful manner, but she felt uneasy in her presence. She was ashamed to have her see the patched dressing jacket that had been packed for her by mistake. She was ashamed of the very patches and darns she had been so proud of at home. At home it had been perfectly clear that for six dressing jackets one needed twenty-four yards of nainsook at sixteen pence the yard, which came to thirty shillings, plus the cutting and the sewing — and that thirty shillings had been saved. But in front of the maid she felt, if not exactly ashamed, then certainly uncomfortable.
Darya Alexandrovna was hugely relieved when Annushka, whom she had known for years, walked in. The smart maid was summoned to her mistress, and Annushka stayed with Darya Alexandrovna.

Annushka was obviously delighted at Dolly's arrival and started chattering away without a pause. Dolly noticed that she was longing to share her opinion of her mistress's situation, especially the count's love and devotion to Anna Arkadyevna, but Dolly carefully cut her off whenever she began on that.
"I grew up with Anna Arkadyevna; my lady is dearer to me than anything. Well, it's not for us to judge. And there does seem to be so much love...."
"Be so good as to pour out the water now, please, so I can wash," Darya Alexandrovna cut her short.
"Of course. We keep two women just for washing the small things, but most of the linen is done by machine. The count looks into everything himself. Ah, what a husband!..."
Dolly was glad when Anna came in and put a stop to Annushka's gossip.
Anna had put on a very simple batiste gown. Dolly studied that simple gown closely. She knew what it meant — and what such simplicity cost.
"An old friend," Anna said of Annushka.

Anna was no longer flustered. She was perfectly composed, perfectly at ease. Dolly saw that she had now fully recovered from the impression of her arrival, and had taken on that surface, careless tone which, as it were, closed the door on the compartment that held her deeper feelings and thoughts.
"Well, Anna, and how is your little girl?" Dolly asked.

"Annie?" (That was what she called her little daughter, Anna.) "Very well. She has come along wonderfully. Would you like to see her? Come, I'll show her to you. We had a dreadful time of it," she went on, "over nurses. We had an Italian wet-nurse. A good creature, but so stupid! We wanted to be rid of her, but the baby is so used to her that we've gone on keeping her."
"But how have you managed?..." Dolly was about to ask what surname the little girl would carry; but, noticing a sudden frown on Anna's face, she shifted course.
"How did you manage? Have you weaned her yet?"
But Anna had understood.

"That isn't what you meant to ask, is it? You meant to ask about her surname. Yes? It worries Alexey. She has no name — that is, she is a Karenina," said Anna, dropping her eyelids until nothing showed but the lashes meeting. "But we'll talk about all that later," she said, her face suddenly brightening. "Come, I'll show you. _Elle est très gentille_. She crawls now."

In the nursery, the luxury that had struck Dolly throughout the house struck her even more. There were little go-carts ordered from England, and contraptions for learning to walk, and a sofa shaped like a billiard table, made specifically for crawling, and swings and baths, all of special design and all up to date. They were all English, sturdy, and well made, and obviously very expensive. The room was large, very bright, and very high-ceilinged.

When they walked in, the baby — wearing nothing but her little smock — was sitting in a small armchair at the table, having her dinner of broth, which she was spilling all over her chest. The baby was being fed, and the Russian nursemaid was clearly sharing the meal. Neither the wet-nurse nor the head nurse was there; they were in the next room, from which came the sound of their conversation in the strange French that was their only common language.

Hearing Anna's voice, a smart, tall English nurse with a disagreeable face and a dissolute look came through the door, hurriedly shaking her fair curls, and at once began defending herself, though Anna had said nothing critical. At every word Anna said, the English nurse said hurriedly, several times over, "Yes, my lady."

The rosy baby, with her black eyebrows and dark hair, her sturdy red little body and its tight goose-flesh skin, delighted Darya Alexandrovna in spite of the cross look the child fixed on the stranger. She positively envied the baby's robust health. She was delighted, too, with how the baby crawled. None of her own children had crawled like that. When the baby was set down on the carpet and her little dress was tucked up behind, she was wonderfully charming. She looked around like some small wild animal at the grown-ups with her bright black eyes, smiled — clearly pleased that they were admiring her — and, with her legs splayed sideways, pushed strongly on her arms, then quickly drew her whole back up after them, and made another little advance forward on her arms.

But the whole atmosphere of the nursery, and especially the English nurse, Darya Alexandrovna did not like at all. The only way she could explain to herself how Anna, with her insight into people, could have taken on so unprepossessing, so disreputable-looking a woman as nurse to her child was to assume that no good nurse would have agreed to enter a household as irregular as Anna's.

Besides, from a few stray remarks, Darya Alexandrovna saw at once that Anna, the two nurses, and the child shared no common life, and that the mother's visit was something out of the ordinary. Anna wanted to fetch a plaything for the baby and couldn't find it.
Most astonishing of all was that when Anna was asked how many teeth the baby had, she answered wrong and knew nothing about the two newest ones.

"Sometimes I feel sorry I am so superfluous here," Anna said, leaving the nursery and lifting her skirt to step around the plaything that stood in the doorway. "It was very different with my first child."
"I would have expected the opposite," said Darya Alexandrovna shyly.

"Oh, no! By the way, do you know I saw Seryozha?" Anna said, narrowing her eyes as though looking at something far off. "But we'll talk about that later. You wouldn't believe it — I'm like a hungry beggar woman in front of a full dinner. I don't know what to start on first. The dinner is you, and the conversations I have ahead of me with you, which I could never have with anyone else; and I can't decide which subject to begin on. _Mais je ne vous ferai grâce de rien_. I must have everything out with you."

"Oh, I really ought to give you a sketch of the company you'll meet here," she went on. "I'll start with the ladies. Princess Varvara — you know her, and I know what you and Stiva think of her. Stiva says the entire purpose of her life is to prove her superiority over Auntie Katerina Pavlovna: all true; but she's a good-hearted woman, and I am so grateful to her. In Petersburg there was a moment when I absolutely had to have a chaperone. And then she turned up. But really, she is good-hearted. She did a great deal to ease my position. I see you don't grasp the whole difficulty of my position — there, in Petersburg," she added. "Here I am perfectly at ease and happy. Well, more on that later. Then Sviazhsky — he is the marshal of the district, a very decent sort of man, but he wants something out of Alexey. You understand: with his land, now that we are settled in the country, Alexey can wield great influence. Then there's Tushkevitch — you've met him, you know him — Betsy's admirer. Now he has been dropped and he has come to see us. As Alexey says, he is one of those people who are very pleasant so long as you accept them as what they try to appear to be, _et puis il est comme il faut_, as Princess Varvara says. Then Veslovsky... you know him. A nice boy," she said, and a sly smile curved her lips. "What's this wild story about him and the Levins? Veslovsky told Alexey, and we don't believe a word of it. _Il est très gentil et naïf_," she said, smiling again. "Men need something to do, and Alexey needs a circle, so I value all these people. We have to keep the house lively and amusing, so that Alexey will not long for something new. Then you'll meet the steward — a German, a very good man, and he understands his work. Alexey thinks very highly of him. Then the doctor, a young man — not quite a Nihilist, perhaps, but, you know, eats with his knife... still, a very good doctor. Then the architect.... _Une petite cour!_"
